extracted.intended_audience: meteorologists, field observers, instrument technicians, and evolutionary biologists/naturalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and empirical methods for measuring and correcting wind-induced errors in rain-gauge observations, including protective contrivances (Nipher jacket, Wild fence) and paired-gauge/anemometer correction methods. (The page also contains a separate review of mimicry theory with criteria for evaluating mimicry hypotheses.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Wind exposure effects on rain-gauges
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauges in situations much exposed to the wind invariably indicate a smaller amount of rain than gauges protected from the wind; the decrease of recorded rainfall with elevation is apparent and due to more imperfect catch consequent upon increased exposure to wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wind interferes with proper catch by eddying around the mouth of the gauge; therefore a rain-gauge should, on theoretical principles, be protected from wind disturbance if we would know the true quantity of rain that falls upon the ground in its vicinity. Placement on exposed poles or near edges of buildings/cliffs introduces augmented wind velocity and complex eddies causing undercatch on windward sides and relative surplus leeward. Avoid highly exposed locations where possible; prefer sheltered positions or use protection devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archibald's-law/Abbe correction for height
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed deficit of rain indicated by an elevated gauge was found proportional to the square root of its altitude above the ground, relating to Archibald's law connecting increase of wind velocity with square root of altitude for small altitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Abbe's deduction to estimate numerical wind correction for a rain-gauge in a free open situation; recognize that elevation above ground increases wind velocity (roughly with sqrt(height)) and thus reduces catch. This relationship underpins practical correction formulas and comparison methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paired-gauge (double-height) empirical correction method
rubrics_metrics.description: If a second gauge, similar in all essential respects, be placed twice as high above the ground as the gauge to be corrected, the comparison of their readings can yield a numerical wind correction for the lower gauge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place two similar gauges in approximately similar conditions except for height (one twice the height). From readings over sufficient periods deduce correction to apply to exposed gauge. This forms the basis of Abbe's numerical correction for open situations; it is a practical field test to estimate height-dependent undercatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paired sheltered-vs-exposed long-period correction method (A/B/K equation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrected rainfall at an exposed station may be determined from the rainfall at a nearby sheltered station for a sufficiently long period by using the relative discrepancies during periods of rain and of snow and an empirically determined constant K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent sheltered rainfall as 100, exposed as 100 − A for rain periods and 100 − A − B for snow periods; solve the provided relation for the correction x. K must be empirically determined for the district by establishing two similar gauges close together (one with protection, one free) so that for co-located pairs K ≈ A/B and then x = K B − A. The method applies to many instances and has been tested against a more direct anemometer-based method with concordant results. Values of K for some German localities have ranged from 0.13 to 0.54.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anemometer-based correction and cross-validation
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative, more direct method involves using anemometer readings to reduce measured quantities of precipitation to equal mean wind velocities; results agree closely with paired-gauge correction methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simultaneous wind-speed measurements to normalize gauge catches to a common mean wind velocity; compare outcomes with paired-sheltered/exposed correction — concordant results validate the simpler comparative equation approach. Employ both methods for verification where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical determination of local correction constant K
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of K must be empirically determined for a particular district by side-by-side establishment of two similar rain-gauges, one fitted with efficient wind-protection, the other left free; for gauges close together K may be taken as A/B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run colocated experiments long enough to capture rain and snow conditions; compute A and B (relative discrepancies) to derive K = A/B; use K to correct long-term records of exposed stations by the formula x = K B − A. Expect K to vary by locality (example range 0.13–0.54 reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of wind-protection contrivance: Nipher jacket vs Wild fence
rubrics_metrics.description: The most efficient wind-protection contrivances for rain-gauges are the Nipher jacket and the Wild fence enclosure; the Wild fence is generally more accurate and advantageous in special circumstances though less used than the Nipher jacket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the Wild fence enclosure as the standard of accuracy for wind protection in many cases; use the Nipher jacket in ordinary situations where it is generally well adapted. For very exposed or unsheltered locations, prefer the fence enclosure. Consider practicalities (usage prevalence, maintenance, local snow conditions) when choosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for heating apparatus in Nipher jackets in snowy climates
rubrics_metrics.description: A Nipher gauge ought to be fitted with some form of heating apparatus adequate to prevent accumulations of snow in winter upon the protecting jacket, from which accumulated snow may be blown into the rain-gauge portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In regions with significant snowfall, equip Nipher jackets with heating to avoid snow build-up and blown-in snow contamination of gauges; without heating the effective accuracy of the Nipher jacket can be considerably reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fence enclosure for gauges unduly exposed to wind
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Nipher protector is generally well adapted, it may be advantageously replaced by the Wild fence enclosure in the case of gauges unduly exposed to the full force of the wind in unsheltered locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exposed site conditions produce large wind errors (e.g., open outskirts, near forests or banks), install a fence enclosure: the Wild fence may approximate 100% accuracy (if Wild fence = 100), whereas Nipher may be ~100 in sheltered positions but drop to ~80 or lower in fully exposed positions. Choose fence where maximal accuracy is required despite higher cost/complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for local terrain effects on gauge placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of gauges on buildings or near steep cliffs or banks is more complicated due to disturbances introduced by such obstructions, causing deficits on windward sides and relative surplus leeward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing gauges near structures or abrupt terrain changes that create asymmetric eddies; if unavoidable, characterize the local wind flow and apply correction or relocate to more representative open/sheltered sites. Use experimental comparisons with nearby sheltered gauges to assess local biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: laboratory/experimental study needed to understand wind eddies
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is known as to the mode of formation or complexity of wind eddies around gauges; information could only be suggested through laboratory experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support field observation with controlled laboratory studies (wind-tunnel) to understand eddy formation and design/optimize protective contrivances. Use experimental evidence to inform empirical correction formulas and protective designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish superficial resemblance from structural affinity (mimicry evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimetic resemblances often affect only obvious external characters and are independent of affinity; internal morphology and structural characters may remain distinct despite close external resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether resemblance is due to mimicry or common ancestry, examine internal structures (e.g., wing cell venation, scale shape/number) and not only outward appearance. Superficial similarity that leaves deep morphological differences suggests mimicry (convergent selection) rather than affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess multiple mechanistic routes to the same visual effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar visual outcomes (e.g., wing transparence) in different taxa can be produced by distinct mechanisms (shape/size reduction of scales, diminution in number, scales becoming transparent or vertical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same visual appearance arises via different structural mechanisms across taxa, a direct common environmental cause is unlikely; natural selection acting on predator vision is a more plausible unifying explanation. Investigators should document the proximate anatomical/mechanistic basis of the resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare competing explanations: affinity, direct environmental action, and natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Affinity may explain resemblance within closely related taxa, direct environmental causes have limited explanatory power where mechanisms differ, and natural selection (Batesian and Müllerian) provides an adequate cause if it explains both mimics and models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Occam's razor: prefer the established adequate cause (natural selection) if it can meet the requirements across cases before invoking distinct causes. Evaluate abundance, conspicuousness, flight behavior, and immunity or distastefulness to judge Batesian versus Müllerian mimicry; test for predator learning and shared benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Müllerian predator-learning hypothesis and 'tax' concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Predators (birds) lack instinctive knowledge of palatability and must learn by experience; distasteful species pay a 'tax' (loss) as individuals are sampled until predators learn to avoid them. If distasteful species resemble each other, the learning cost is shared and reduced per species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate Müllerian mimicry, seek evidence that predators learn to avoid distasteful forms and that resemblance reduces per-species mortality. Empirical work (behavioural experiments or field predation rates) supporting predator learning strengthens the Müllerian explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use breeding/offspring evidence to establish conspecific polymorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding diverse mimetic forms among the offspring of one individual demonstrates that the diverse forms are conspecific (example: Papilio/Papilio dardanus females showing multiple mimetic forms among offspring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct breeding and rearing studies where possible to demonstrate that different forms are alternative morphs of the same species rather than distinct species; this informs interpretation of female-limited mimicry and intraspecific polymorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic variation as diagnostic for cause of resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of mimetic assemblages change hue and pattern together across geographic regions (regional facies), which may reflect selective regimes tied to local predator communities and supports natural-selection explanations over uniform external causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document geographic races and correlated changes across taxa in the same assemblage; concordant geographic shifts in pattern across unrelated taxa imply shared selective pressures (predator-mediated) rather than purely local environmental painting/sculpting effects.
